title: How does post-shuffle partition coalescing work — Spark creates N shuffle partitions initially, observes actual sizes at runtime, and merges small partitions to reduce task overhead — and what config controls it (`spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled`)?

s1_definition.profdef: Post-shuffle partition coalescing is an AQE optimization where Spark initially creates a fixed large number of shuffle partitions, then at runtime observes their actual sizes and merges adjacent small partitions into fewer, larger ones that approach a target size, reducing the number of tasks in the following stage and cutting scheduling overhead. It is governed by `spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled`, together with `spark.sql.adaptive.enabled`, and tuned by the advisory partition size and minimum partition number settings.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine after a big re-sort at the National Bank of India, the rule was to always split work into two hundred trays regardless of volume. On a quiet day, most trays hold just a few slips, so you have two hundred clerks each doing almost nothing — all the time goes into handing out and collecting trays, not actual work. Coalescing is the supervisor noticing this and combining the near-empty trays into, say, eight full trays, so eight clerks do real work and you stop wasting effort shuffling empty trays around. On a busy day the trays are already full, so he leaves them alone.
s1_definition.oneliner: Coalescing starts with many fixed shuffle partitions, then merges the small ones at runtime into fewer balanced partitions so the next stage has fewer, right-sized tasks — switched on by the adaptive coalesce setting.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Post-shuffle partition coalescing is an AQE optimization where Spark initially creates a fixed large number of shuffle partitions, then at runtime observes their actual sizes and merges adjacent small partitions into fewer, larger ones that approach a target size, reducing the number of tasks in the following stage and cutting scheduling overhead. It is governed by `spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled`, together with `spark.sql.adaptive.enabled`, and tuned by the advisory partition size and minimum partition number settings.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine after a big re-sort at the National Bank of India, the rule was to always split work into two hundred trays regardless of volume. On a quiet day, most trays hold just a few slips, so you have two hundred clerks each doing almost nothing — all the time goes into handing out and collecting trays, not actual work. Coalescing is the supervisor noticing this and combining the near-empty trays into, say, eight full trays, so eight clerks do real work and you stop wasting effort shuffling empty trays around. On a busy day the trays are already full, so he leaves them alone.

**One line to remember:** Coalescing starts with many fixed shuffle partitions, then merges the small ones at runtime into fewer balanced partitions so the next stage has fewer, right-sized tasks — switched on by the adaptive coalesce setting.

sections.s2_technical:
The root problem is that the number of shuffle partitions is a static configuration, the shuffle-partitions setting, which defaults to two hundred. This single number applies to every shuffle in the job regardless of how much data actually flows through it. For a large dataset two hundred might be too few, but for a dataset that has been heavily filtered or aggregated it is often far too many, leaving most of the two hundred partitions nearly empty. Since Spark runs one task per partition in the next stage, you then launch roughly two hundred tasks that each process almost nothing, and the fixed per-task overhead — scheduling, serialization, launching — dominates, so the stage is slow for no good reason.

Coalescing fixes this using the fact that a shuffle is a natural checkpoint where real sizes are known. Spark still writes the initial large number of shuffle partitions, but before the next stage reads them, AQE looks at the actual size of each partition. It then groups contiguous partitions together so that each coalesced group is close to a configured target, the advisory partition size, often tens of megabytes. The next stage reads these merged groups, so instead of two hundred tiny tasks you might get eight well-sized tasks, each doing a meaningful amount of work with far less overhead in total.

Several settings control the behavior. The master switch is the adaptive-enabled setting, and coalescing specifically is the coalesce-partitions-enabled setting, both on by default in modern Spark. The advisory partition size sets the target size for each coalesced partition, and a minimum partition number setting prevents coalescing from collapsing everything into too few partitions, which would under-use the cluster. Spark coalesces only contiguous partitions to preserve any ordering guarantees from the shuffle.

A senior nuance is that coalescing reduces the task count but does not increase it, so it addresses the too-many-small-partitions problem, not the too-few-huge-partitions problem — for that you need a higher initial shuffle-partitions value or repartitioning. It also pairs naturally with skew handling, which goes the other way by splitting oversized partitions, so together they drive partitions toward a balanced target from both directions. Another practical point is that coalescing is why you can usually leave the shuffle-partitions setting high and let AQE bring it down adaptively, rather than hand-tuning it per job. In the bank, coalescing removed the chronic slowness of our post-aggregation stages, where a filtered daily slice produced a handful of real partitions but two hundred scheduled tasks.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A fixed two hundred shuffle partitions leaves most nearly empty after filtering. This is exactly the overhead problem coalescing solves.

Problem 2 — The next stage runs two hundred tasks doing almost nothing. This is exactly why merging into fewer right-sized partitions helps.

Problem 3 — The team wants one knob to control this rather than hand-tuning each job. This is exactly the role of the coalesce settings.

The mini-project models coalescing in Java. A `ShuffleWriter` produces a fixed number of partitions with realistic skewed-small sizes. A `PartitionCoalescer` reads the actual sizes and merges contiguous small partitions toward a target advisory size, respecting a minimum partition count. The demo processes a filtered daily slice of Rajesh's and Priya's transactions and shows the task count before and after coalescing.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a filtered daily slice that, after the shuffle, is written into the static two hundred partitions, each only about zero point two to one megabyte, totalling roughly a hundred megabytes. The advisory target per coalesced partition is sixty-four megabytes.

Step 1: The shuffle writer produces the fixed two hundred partitions because the shuffle-partitions setting is two hundred, regardless of the small data volume. This is the static behavior before AQE acts.

Step 2: Without coalescing, the next stage would run two hundred tasks to process only about a hundred megabytes, so each task handles well under a megabyte and the per-task overhead dominates — this is the inefficiency.

Step 3: Coalescing reads the actual sizes of all two hundred partitions at the shuffle boundary. It walks them in order, accumulating sizes.

Step 4: Whenever the accumulated size reaches the sixty-four-megabyte target, it closes a coalesced group and starts a new one. Roughly a hundred megabytes of tiny partitions therefore collapse into about two groups near the target, plus a small final group.

Step 5: The next stage now runs just a couple of tasks instead of two hundred, each processing a meaningful chunk, which slashes total scheduling and launch overhead while doing the identical work.

Step 6: The journey shows the static two hundred partitions reduced adaptively to a handful of balanced ones, which is exactly the win the coalesce setting provides on filtered or aggregated data.

```text
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] shuffle wrote fixed 200 partitions (static config)
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] WITHOUT coalescing: next stage = 200 tasks for only 119 MB of data
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] coalesced 200 partitions => 2 (target 64000000B)
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] WITH coalescing: next stage = 2 tasks (far less overhead)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Shuffle (static config: spark.sql.shuffle.partitions = 200)
  P0(0.5MB) P1(0.3MB) P2(0.9MB) ... P199(0.4MB)   ← 200 tiny partitions, ~119MB total
    │
    ▼  AQE coalescePartitions.enabled = true (read real sizes at boundary)
  accumulate contiguous partitions toward advisory 64MB:
  [P0..P~120 ≈ 64MB] [P~121..P199 ≈ 55MB]
    │
    ▼
  Next stage: 2 tasks (instead of 200) — same data, tiny overhead
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Post-shuffle partition coalescing is an AQE optimization that fixes a very common inefficiency caused by the shuffle-partitions setting being a single static number, defaulting to two hundred, that applies to every shuffle regardless of data volume. After a heavy filter or aggregation, those two hundred partitions often end up nearly empty, and because Spark runs one task per partition in the next stage, you launch roughly two hundred tasks that each process almost nothing, so the fixed per-task overhead of scheduling and launching dominates and the stage is slow for no real reason.

Coalescing works by using the shuffle as a natural checkpoint. Spark still writes the initial fixed number of partitions, but before the next stage reads them, AQE looks at the actual size of each partition and merges contiguous small ones into fewer groups that each approach a configured target, the advisory partition size. So two hundred tiny partitions might become eight well-sized ones, and the next stage runs eight meaningful tasks instead of two hundred trivial ones, doing the identical work with far less overhead. It is controlled by the adaptive-enabled master switch together with the coalesce-partitions-enabled setting, both on by default, with the advisory partition size setting the target and a minimum partition number preventing it from collapsing too far; Spark only merges contiguous partitions so any shuffle ordering is preserved.

In my project at the National Bank of India this removed the chronic slowness of our post-aggregation stages, where a filtered daily slice produced only a handful of partitions worth of real data but still scheduled two hundred tasks. The practical lesson I share is that coalescing is why you can usually leave the shuffle-partitions value high and let AQE bring the task count down adaptively per stage, rather than hand-tuning it for every job. I also point out that coalescing only reduces partitions, so it solves the too-many-tiny-partitions case, not the too-few-huge-partitions case, and it pairs with AQE's skew splitting, which goes the opposite way, so together they push partitions toward a balanced target from both directions.
